content.text: Creating a Git branch doesn't copy your project. A branch is a 41-byte file holding the hash of one commit, and every commit already points to a full snapshot of the project.

and commits. An hour later a production bug comes in. She fixes it on

The belief: a branch is a separate copy of the project. Creating one duplicates the files somewhere, and from then on you work "inside" that copy, safely away from

Smart people believe it for good reasons. Many older version control systems did branch that way: Pro Git describes the way "most older VCS tools" branch as "copying all of the project's files into a second directory." Branch diagrams show two lines splitting apart. And when you switch branches, your editor really does show different files, as if you had opened another folder.
The half-truth: each branch does give you a complete version of the project. But that version lives in commits Git already stores, not in a new folder, and creating a branch doesn't put you on it.
A commit is a snapshot of the whole project
Git doesn't store a list of edits. Pro Git says that every time you commit, Git "takes a picture of what all your files look like at that moment and stores a reference to that snapshot." A

object points to that snapshot (a tree of file contents), records the author and the message, and points to its parent commit. Files that didn't change aren't stored again; the new snapshot links to the identical version Git already has.
A branch is a 41-byte file that names a commit
is, in Pro Git's words, "simply a lightweight movable pointer to one of these commits." On disk it's a file under
holding the commit's 40-character SHA-1 hash, so creating one is "as quick and simple as writing 41 bytes to a file (40 characters and a newline)." That's why
returns instantly in a repository of any size: it writes one tiny file pointing at the current commit, and nothing is copied.
Git knows which branch you're on through a special pointer,

doesn't hold a hash at all; it names a branch. When you commit, Git stores the new commit with the current one as its parent, then moves the branch that HEAD names. Every other branch stays exactly where it was. And the
docs say plainly that creating a branch "will not switch the working tree to it".
Here's the shop repository from the story, before Mona's experiment, on Git 2.54:

blocks.code:
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main
# 36711c7c6d478c5eb8f29c6ff7c3beebc036cac6
wc -c < .git/refs/heads/main
# 41
git cat-file -p main
# tree 46cdfae862269f28526542085304f7cdd36cfc85
# parent ad5a0fce7e79f05179f4d6f3da3d2f00a72539f7
# author Dev <dev@example.com> 1793736859 +0200
# committer Dev <dev@example.com> 1793736859 +0200
#
# Reject empty carts

content.text: is a 41-byte file holding a hash. The commit it points to records a tree (the snapshot), a parent, an author and a message. Nowhere is there a folder per branch.
Switching rewrites your one working tree
There's one working tree: the files you edit.

moves HEAD to another branch, and, as its docs put it, "the working tree and the index are updated to match the branch." Your files change because Git rewrites them from that branch's snapshot, not because you stepped into another folder. Uncommitted edits don't belong to any branch, so Git carries them along when it can. If you really need two branches on disk at once, that's what a
is for: a second working directory attached to the same repository.
The fix: create the pointer and move HEAD to it
Here's Mona's session, replayed in that repository, next to the one that does what she meant:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
git branch refactor   # "make a copy to experiment in"
git log --oneline --decorate
# 36711c7 (HEAD -> main, refactor) Reject empty carts
# ad5a0fc Add checkout
git commit -am "Compute total from items"
# [main 5fd5bc8] Compute total from items
#  1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
git log --oneline --decorate -2
# 5fd5bc8 (HEAD -> main) Compute total from items
# 36711c7 (refactor) Reject empty carts

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
git switch -c refactor   # create the pointer AND move HEAD to it
# Switched to a new branch 'refactor'
git commit -am "Compute total from items"
# [refactor 64309fb] Compute total from items
#  1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
git log --oneline --decorate --all -2
# 64309fb (HEAD -> refactor) Compute total from items
# 36711c7 (main) Reject empty carts
git switch main   # the files go back to main's snapshot
# Switched to branch 'main'

items.title: Use a worktree instead of copying the folder

content.text: When you need two branches open at once, say a hotfix while a refactor is half done, add a git worktree: a second directory on the same repository, so commits made in either land in the same history.
